lexicon: delve
- `look at` or `read` when someone examined code or documents.
- `test` / `measure` / `profile` when there was an experiment; name it.
- `compare` when two things were set side by side; give both results.
- Cut it when the sentence works with the verb removed: start with the finding.
leverage
- `use` in almost every case.
- `build on`, `reuse`, `call` when you want to say which part does the work.
- Cut it when the tool name already carries the sentence.
utilize
- `use` everywhere.
- Name the action when "use" is still vague: "reads from", "writes to", "calls".
- Cut it when the tool can be the subject of the sentence.
harness
- `use` for the plain act.
- Say what the thing does: "drafts", "flags", "runs on".
- `run on` when the hardware or service is the point: "runs on a single A100".
- Cut it and lead with the result.
unlock
- `lets you` or `you can now`, followed by the action.
- `includes` for plan comparisons: say what the plan includes.
- Cut it when the result can be named directly.
unleash
- Name the capability and the count: "200 templates for invoices and posters".
- `runs on`, `uses all` for performance claims, with a measurement.
- Cut it; the noun phrase after it is usually the real content.
elevate
- `improve`, plus what changed and by how much.
- `raise` for a number: raise the timeout, raise the contrast ratio.
- Cut it and describe the detail itself.
empower
- `lets` or `helps`, followed by the specific action.
- Name the mechanism: "with preview deploys", "with shared drafts".
- Cut everything before "to" and keep the verb phrase.
streamline
- `cut`, `remove`, `merge`, with the count of steps.
- `simplify` only next to what got removed.
- In commits, name the change: "remove", "inline", "merge".
- `automate`, with the step that no longer needs a person.
revolutionize
- Say what is different, compared with what the reader uses now.
- `replaces` when it does replace a step or a tool.
- Cut it; a plain description of the change carries more weight.
supercharge
- `speeds up`, with the measured gain.
- Name the feature: "adds fuzzy search", "adds tabs".
- Cut it and lead with the feature.
embark
- `start`, `begin`.
- Name the first step instead of the trip.
- Cut it: "Before migrating" works on its own.
navigate
- `go to`, `open` in UI instructions.
- `handle`, `deal with`, `get through` for problems, or name the problem.
- `find` when the reader is looking for something in a list or a menu.
- Cut it and give the step.
foster
- Name the rule or the practice: "we reply to every first PR within 3 days".
- `helps`, `leads to`, with the effect.
- Cut it when the practice can stand alone.
cultivate
- `build` or `grow`, only next to the method.
- In résumés, `hired`, `trained`, `kept`, with counts.
- Cut it and state the habit.
underscore
- `shows`, followed by what it shows.
- State the action item instead of the moral.
- `confirms`, only when an earlier claim was tested and held.
- Cut the sentence when it repeats the one before.
showcase
- `shows` or `demonstrates`, with what exactly.
- Describe the project: what it does, who used it, one number.
- For the noun, `gallery`, `examples`, `demo`.
spearhead
- `led`, `ran`, `started`, with scope.
- Name your part: "wrote the plan", "did the cutover".
- Add the result and its number.
bolster
- `add` or `strengthen`, with the specific change.
- `increase`, with a number.
- Cut it and list the changes.
amplify
- `increase` or `reach more people`, with a number.
- Name the effect with its unit: "cuts p95 latency from 900ms to 120ms".
- `share`, `repost`, `pay`, for what an organization actually does.
- `repeat` or `retweet`, when that is the actual action.
catalyze
- `start`, `cause`, `lead to`, with the result.
- `fund` or `pay for` when money is the mechanism.
- Cut it and give the sequence of events.
illuminate
- `explains` or `shows`, with the claim.
- `found`, for investigations, followed by the findings.
- Cut it and state the point that was learned.
resonate
- Report the evidence: "6 of 8 people in testing chose it".
- `matches` or `fits` for brand rules, with the rule.
- In letters, give the specific reason in one sentence.
transcend
- `outlasts` or `goes beyond`, only with what is passed and how.
- Name the limit that was removed.
- Cut it and describe what the thing is.
reimagine
- `redesigned`, plus the list of changes.
- `rebuilt` when the code was rewritten.
- `new version` or `remake` for games and media.
redefine
- State the old expectation and the new fact.
- Give the spec that is unusual.
- Cut the tagline and use the spec as the headline.
reshape
- `changes`, with the specific change and its source.
- Give a number with a date.
- Cut the scene-setting sentence and start with the evidence.
envision
- `plan`, `want`, `expect`, with a date.
- In RFCs, write the goals and the non-goals.
- Cut the vision and state what ships next.
curate
- `pick`, `select`, `choose`, with the rule.
- `edit` for newsletters.
- `review` for a quality check, with the criteria.
embrace
- `adopt`, `switch to`, `start using`, with the reason.
- `accept` for an attitude, then name the practice.
- `try`, when the decision is still an experiment; give the end date.
- Cut it and give the decision with its date.
enhance
- `improve`, with the number.
- Say what changed: "added", "fixed", "faster".
- In changelogs, one line per change, each with its own verb.
- `fix` for bugs; a fixed bug is not an improvement in general terms.
enrich
- `add`, with the fields or content added.
- `join` or `look up` for data pipelines.
- Cut the adjective and describe the program.
facilitate
- `lets`, `helps`, `allows`, with the action.
- `run` or `lead` for meetings and workshops.
- Name the mechanism: "sends", "exposes", "proxies".
optimize
- `make X faster` or `cut X`, with numbers and the method.
- For screen sizes, name the widths you tested.
- In commits, name the change: "add index on `orders.user_id`".
- `tune` for a config change, with the parameter and its old and new value.
maximize
- `increase`, with the measure and the target.
- Name the steps instead of the goal.
- Cut it and state the result someone measured.
ideate
- `brainstorm`, `come up with`, `sketch`, with the count.
- Name the method: "crazy eights", "a list of 30 headlines".
- Report which idea won and why.
democratize
- `make cheaper` or `make free`, with the old and new price.
- `make easier`, with the skill no longer needed.
- Name who can now use it and how many do.
future-proof
- Name the change the design allows: "add a payment provider without touching checkout".
- Give support dates: "security updates until 2031".
- `plan for`, with the specific plan.
unpack
- `explain`, `go through`.
- Instead of "a lot", say how many points and list them.
- Cut it and give the first point.
immerse
- Describe what is on screen or in the room.
- Give the hours, the format, the ratio.
- Cut it and start with the activity.
captivate
- `hold attention`, only with how it was measured.
- Report sales, reads, or completion rates.
- Describe the content that would do the work.
mesmerize
- Describe the motion: speed, count, what triggers it.
- Describe the scene in concrete terms.
- Cut it, then ask whether the effect is needed at all.
ignite
- `start` or `lead to`, with the result.
- Report the measurable effect.
- Cut it and describe the course or event.
propel
- `help` or `lead to`, with the chain of cause and effect.
- Report the change and the period.
- Cut it and say what the product does.
skyrocket
- `rose`, `grew`, `doubled`, with the numbers and dates.
- Give the start and end values.
- Cut the verb and show the chart with labeled axes.
boost
- `increase` or `raise`, with the measured change.
- `faster`, with the benchmark and its conditions.
- `help`, only next to what helped and by how much.
- Cut it and name the thing done.
fuel
- `caused`, `led to`, `pushed up`, with the evidence.
- `pays for` or `funds` when money is meant.
- Cut the bio joke.
intertwine
- `depends on`, `affects`, `is part of`, with the direction.
- `linked`, only next to the link.
- Name the shared cause.
underpin
- `is based on`, `uses`, `runs on`.
- List the principles themselves.
- Cut it and say what depends on what.
encompass
- `includes`, `covers`.
- List the items, then what is out of scope.
- `spans` for ranges of time or numbers, with the two ends.
- Cut it and make the list the sentence.
epitomize
- `is an example of` or `is typical of`, then say why.
- In reviews, name the action.
- Cut it and describe the example.
exemplify
- `shows` or `is an example of`.
- Name the practice the example follows.
- For snippets, write "For example" and show the code.
embody
- `shows`, `has`, `follows`, with the specific trait.
- Describe the object.
- Cut the abstract claim.
encapsulate
- `sums up` for summaries, or just give the summary.
- `wraps`, `contains`, `hides` in code, and say what callers no longer see.
- Cut it.
burgeon
- `growing`, with the rate.
- Give a count and a date.
- Cut the adjective; the topic does not need it.
flourish
- `grow`, with the measure.
- For the noun, name the detail.
- Cut it.
thrive
- `do well`, only with the measure.
- Name what the place offers: pay, hours, promotion path.
- Describe the result.
- `grow`, `survive`, `stay open`, with a number and a period.
garner
- `got`, `received`, `has`.
- Give the number and the source.
- Cut it when the count is the only content.
boast
- `has`, `includes`, `comes with`.
- Give the number and the comparison.
- Cut it and use a list.
herald
- `announces`, `marks`, `starts`, only with the fact.
- Report who said what: "three analysts called it".
- Cut it and describe the release.
usher
- `started` or `led to`, with what followed.
- Describe the change with a date and a number.
- `opened` or `began`, with a date, for an event that started something.
- Cut the phrase.
elucidate
- `explain`, `show`, `clarify`.
- In papers, state the mechanism found.
- Cut the lead-in and give the example.
disrupt
- Say what you sell, to whom, at what price, against the old option.
- `compete with`, with the competitor's name.
- `replace`, when buyers drop an old product for yours; give the count.
- Cut it.
level up
- Name the skill: "write grid layouts without media queries".
- `learn` or `get better at`, with the topic.
- Cut it and state the outcome.
dive into
- `cover`, `look at`, `explain`.
- If an overview is needed, give it without the announcement.
- Cut it and show the code.
deep dive
- Name the scope: "how B-tree, GIN, and BRIN indexes store data".
- `review`, `walkthrough`, `meeting` for calendar items.
- Cut it from titles; the topic is the title.
lean into
- `focus on`, `do more of`, `commit to`, with the specific choice.
- Name what you will stop doing to make room.
- Cut it and state the plan.
reach out
- `email`, `call`, `message`, `open an issue`, with the address or link.
- `contact` when the channel varies.
- `ask`, when you want something from the reader; say what.
- Cut the polite closer and give the address.
weave
- `combine`, `include`, `connect`, with how.
- For processes, name the step where it happens.
- For fiction, describe the structure.
orchestrate
- `coordinated`, `planned`, `ran` in résumés, with scope.
- Name the scheduler or the control flow: "Kubernetes schedules", "a loop calls".
- `runs`, `calls`, `starts`, in order.
- `schedule`, for jobs with a time or a trigger.
seamless
- The step count: "connects to GitHub in two clicks, with no API key". Use when setup is short enough to count.
- The step that no longer happens: "no second login when you switch from Mail to Calendar". Use for single sign-on and shared sessions.
- The delay: "edits reach your other devices within 2 seconds". Use for sync claims.
- The named list: "works with Slack, Linear and Jira". Use when the claim was about compatibility.
- Cut it when the sentence still says what connects to what without it.
robust
- The failure it survives: "retries failed uploads 3 times with exponential backoff". Use for error handling.
- The measured limit: "tested at 12,000 requests per second on one 4-core node". Use for performance.
- The uptime record: "99.95% uptime over the last 12 months, status page linked". Use for hosting.
- The test that tried to break it: "fuzzed with 2 million malformed inputs, no crashes". Use for parsers and protocols.
- Cut it when the sentence describes a feature and the adjective only adds praise.
comprehensive
- The count: "covers 14 commands, from `docker build` to `docker compose down`". Use for guides.
- The coverage figure: "line coverage for `billing/` went from 41% to 88%". Use for tests.
- The scope and its edge: "covers Linux and macOS; Windows is out of scope". Use when readers need to know what is missing.
- The named parts: "invoicing, payroll and expense reports". Use for product suites.
- Cut it when the list that follows already shows the scope.
cutting-edge
- The named technology and its date: "uses Whisper large-v3, released November 2023". Use for model and AI claims.
- The benchmark: "scores 71% on SWE-bench Verified". Use when a public benchmark exists.
- The first: "the first open-source tool to read Parquet files in the browser". Use only when you can show it was first.
- What the team publishes or ships: "2 to 3 papers a year on speech recognition". Use for bios.
- Cut it when the sentence already names the technology.
innovative
- The departure from the default: "tasks have no due dates; each gets a weekly time budget instead". Use when there is a real departure.
- The old way it replaces: "a 3-line written update instead of the weekly status meeting". Use for process products.
- The patent or paper: "patent US 11,234,567 covers the sorting method". Use only when it exists.
- Cut it when you cannot name the new thing, because then the word is false.
groundbreaking
- The result with its size: "participants recalled 23% more words after 8 hours of sleep than after 4". Use for research.
- The change in plain terms: "the inbox now groups mail by sender, not by date". Use for features.
- Outside confirmation: "cited by 140 papers since 2022". Use only when true.
- Cut it in release notes and list the changes instead.
game-changing
- The before and after: "builds that took 11 minutes now take 90 seconds". Use when you have a timing.
- The task it removes: "you no longer write migration files by hand". Use when a manual step disappears.
- A named customer's number: "Acme cut duplicate tickets by 30% in the first month". Use with the customer's permission.
- Cut it when the next sentence gives the result, since the phrase only delays it.
transformative
- The outcome with a number: "82% of last year's cohort were promoted within 18 months". Use for education.
- The process that changed: "urgent scans are read first, cutting the wait from 9 days to 2". Use for operations.
- What the partner paid for or did: "3 new clinics and 40 trained nurses in 2024". Use for partnerships.
- Cut it when there is no outcome yet; say what you expect and when you will measure it.
revolutionary
- The mechanism: "type [[ and a title to link two notes". Use for software features.
- The new spec beside the old one: "18 hours of video playback, up from 11". Use for hardware.
- What the person does: "set a limit per category and the card declines past it". Use for consumer finance.
- Cut it in any headline. A headline needs a verb and a noun more than it needs praise.
pivotal
- What the person did: "she signed the first 40 customers herself". Use for biographies.
- The dependency: "no price change ships until the analytics team checks it". Use for process descriptions.
- The event of that year: "in 2019 the team moved from contracts to subscriptions". Use for timelines.
- Cut it whenever "role" follows, and write the role.
crucial
- The consequence: "upgrading without a backup can lose every row since the last snapshot". Use for warnings.
- The imperative alone: "Back up the database before you upgrade." Use for instructions; the order of the steps is the emphasis.
- The finding: "62% of carts are abandoned on the shipping-cost page". Use for research summaries.
- The practice: "post a written update by 10:00 each day". Use for advice.
- Cut it whenever `it is crucial to` opens a sentence, and start with the verb.
vital
- The effect with a figure and source: "below 6 hours of sleep, reaction times slow". Use for health claims.
- The risk: "the CVE fixed in lodash 4.17.21 allows prototype pollution". Use for security advice.
- The metric by name: "Largest Contentful Paint under 2.5 s". Use for performance.
- Cut it when the advice stands on its own.
essential
- Required or optional, stated as such: "Required: Node 20. Optional: Docker, for the local database." Use in setup guides.
- The count and whose list it is: "the 6 extensions I install on every new machine". Use for lists.
- What breaks without it: "without Git you cannot open a pull request". Use when necessity is the point.
- Cut it in feature lists and list the features.
paramount
- The practice: "we do not sell personal data, and we delete accounts within 30 days of a request". Use for privacy.
- The control: "data encrypted at rest with AES-256; staff access requires a hardware key". Use for security.
- The tradeoff you made: "we delayed launch 6 weeks to finish the security audit". Use when you can prove the ranking.
- Cut it when the sentence only says that something matters to you.
multifaceted
- The named parts: "rising food prices, insurance costs and migration". Use for issues.
- The specific skills: "she has shipped iOS apps and run a 6-person support team". Use for people.
- The layers: "single sign-on, per-role permissions and audit logs". Use for security.
- Cut it when a list follows, because the list is the proof.
intricate
- The count: "the service imports 14 packages, 3 of them in a cycle". Use for systems.
- The measurable detail: "120 knots per square inch, dyed with madder and indigo". Use for craft.
- The structure: "two timelines, 1962 and 2012, that meet in the last chapter". Use for plots.
- Cut it when the noun already implies many parts.
nuanced
- The conditions: "remote work raised output for senior writers and lowered it for new hires". Use when the answer depends on cases.
- The demonstrated knowledge: "he priced 3 product lines and predicted the 2023 drop". Use for people.
- The rule and its exception: "we remove slurs; we keep quoted slurs in news reporting". Use for policies.
- Cut it when you give the cases anyway.
holistic

- The specific services: "physiotherapy and sleep coaching". Use for health providers.

- The refresh rule: "charts reload every 30 seconds from the live database". Use for dashboards.
- The runtime behavior: "routes are read from `routes.json` at startup". Use for technical docs.

- The values: "accent #B4441C on page #F7F5F0". Use for color.

- The list of places: "4 galleries, a repertory cinema and a weekly open mic". Use for towns.

meticulous
- The error rate or audit result: "no billing errors across 3,000 invoices in 2024". Use for CVs.
- The process step: "one person stitches each bag and a second checks it against 12 points". Use for products.
- What was checked and what was not: "read all 4 changed files and ran the tests; did not check the migrations". Use for code review.
- Cut it when describing yourself, and give the record.
unparalleled
- The fact behind the view: "every room faces south toward Mont Blanc". Use for hospitality.
- The benchmark with the rival named: "40% faster than Postgres 16 on TPC-H, same hardware". Use for performance, with the scripts published.
- The support terms: "a named engineer replies within 1 hour, any time of day". Use for service.
- Cut it when you have no comparison, because a superlative without one is empty.
unprecedented
- The record and the previous record: "1.2 million sign-ups, three times the old monthly high". Use for growth.
- The practical facts of the crisis: "stores closed until 15 May; orders still ship in 2 days". Use for customer emails.

unwavering
- The record over time: "a security fix within 48 hours of every report since 2016". Use for commitments.
- What the person did: "you read every draft within a day for 3 years". Use for thanks.
- The events: "she rebuilt the lab twice, after the floods of 2011 and 2014". Use for tributes.
- Cut it in thanks and say what you are thankful for.
unmatched
- The spec: "240 Hz panel, 1 ms response time". Use for hardware.
- The tenure and count: "payroll for 1,800 dental clinics since 2009". Use for experience.
- The price and what it includes: "12 USD per user, single sign-on included". Use for value.

compelling
- The argument: "switching cuts a typical hosting bill from 900 to 340 USD a month". Use for persuasion.
- The trait of the story: "open on one named customer and one problem, in under 50 words". Use for writing advice.
- The finding: "returns fell 18% after we added size charts". Use for data.

captivating
- The premise: "a widowed beekeeper learns her husband had a second family". Use for blurbs.
- The visual spec: "full-width photos at 2400 px, captions below, never on top". Use for design.
- The moment: "her 4-minute monologue in Act 2 drew applause mid-scene". Use for reviews.
- Cut it when the description follows.
stunning
- The output and the time: "a 5-page site from a template in about 20 minutes". Use for site builders.
- What is in the picture: "the sea is visible from the kitchen and living room". Use for property.
- The output size: "2048 by 2048 px from a text prompt". Use for image tools.
- Cut it when the image is shown, because the image already makes the case.
breathtaking
- What you see, and from where: "the lake, from the balcony and both bedrooms". Use for listings.
- The route facts: "11 km, 900 m of climbing, about 5 hours". Use for hikes.
- The measure of simplicity: "one config file, 12 lines". Use when the sense was "simple".
- Cut it every time; there is no case where it adds a fact.
enchanting
- The physical facts: "a hilltop village of 400 people, 30 minutes from Avignon". Use for places.
- Capacity and setting: "a walled garden for 120 guests, with a covered terrace". Use for venues.
- Age and length: "a 6-minute read for ages 3 to 5". Use for children's books.
- Cut it when the noun is enough.
awe-inspiring
- The scale: "1.8 km deep and up to 29 km across". Use for canyons, cliffs and mountains.
- The construction facts: "built 1220 to 1258; the nave is 42 m high". Use for buildings.
- What was announced: "3 products and a 30% price cut". Use for events.
- Cut it in recaps and report what happened.
remarkable
- The number with a baseline: "94.1% accuracy, against 88.3% for the previous best". Use for results.
- The deed: "grew the team from 4 to 30 in 2 years and lost no one". Use for references.
- The outcome with its cause: "churn fell from 6% to 2% after onboarding calls began". Use for case studies.
- Cut it when the number is present.
exceptional
- The service level: "median first reply 6 minutes, 7 days a week". Use for support.
- The material and construction: "full-grain leather, 8 stitches per inch". Use for goods.
- The work: "cut CI time from 40 to 9 minutes and wrote the deploy tool". Use for reviews.
- Cut it when "good" would have done, and then write the evidence instead.
extraordinary
- The team's output: "9 people who build the app 2 million nurses use". Use for team pages.
- The program: "90 minutes of Bach cantatas by a 12-voice choir". Use for events.
- The adoption figure: "her method is used in 60% of new trials". Use for impact.
- Cut it in pairs; a repeated intensifier doubles nothing.
profound
- The effect with a measure and a source: "64% of parents in our survey of 1,200". Use for social claims.
- The question itself, stated as a question the paper answers. Use for philosophy.
- The change with dates: "38% of desk roles allowed full remote work in 2024, up from 9% in 2019". Use for trends.
- Cut it when the claim follows.
invaluable
- What the feedback changed: "three reports like yours led to the fixes in 2.3.1". Use for thanks and survey prompts.
- Who it helps and how: "explains each Git command with one diagram". Use for resources.
- The contribution: "she wrote the parser and reviewed 300 pull requests". Use for credit.
- Cut it in survey prompts and ask the question.
indispensable
- How often it is used: "I open it about 40 times a day". Use for tool reviews.
- What the person owns: "within 3 months he owned the billing service and its on-call rotation". Use for references.
- The count and the source: "7 lessons from founders who raised a seed round in 2023". Use for lists.
- Cut it whenever a working alternative exists.
instrumental
- The verb of what they did: "wrote the launch plan and ran the beta with 40 customers". Use for credit.
- The partner's act: "resold the product to 300 schools". Use for partnerships.
- The action and its result: "ran the training that took weekly users from 200 to 1,400". Use for adoption.
- Cut it every time it comes with "in", and write the verb.
integral
- The role: "you will own the checkout service and join on-call in month 2". Use for job ads.
- The rule: "no pull request merges unless CI passes and one reviewer approves". Use for process.
- The practice with a number: "52% of our packaging is recycled cardboard". Use for policy claims.
- Cut it when "part of" can be replaced by a verb.
intuitive
- The test result: "5 of 6 first-time users sent an invoice without help". Use when you ran a test.
- The interaction: "drag a block to move it; press Delete to remove it". Use for editors.
- The borrowed convention: "the same keyboard shortcuts as Google Docs". Use when it follows a known model.
- Cut it in design reviews and describe what a first-time user did.
user-friendly
- The task and the time: "connect a bank and see last month's spending in under 3 minutes". Use for apps.
- The developer facts: "one POST request per charge; every error names the field to fix". Use for APIs.
- The accessibility facts: "every action reachable by keyboard, tested with VoiceOver and NVDA". Use for procurement.
- Cut it when the reader can try the product instead of reading about it.
frictionless
- The screen count: "checkout on one screen, with Apple Pay and saved cards". Use for payments.
- The removed step: "no email confirmation before your first project". Use for onboarding.
- The integration size: "card payments in 14 lines of code". Use for SDKs.
- Cut it whenever steps remain, and count them instead.
effortless
- The setup time: "a project board from a template in about 4 minutes". Use for tools.
- The garment facts: "linen-cotton, machine wash at 30 C, no ironing". Use for clothing.
- The command and its duration: "`fly deploy` builds and ships in about 90 seconds". Use for developer tools.
- Cut it in how-tos; the steps show how much effort the task takes.
delightful
- The specific detail: "the checkbox fills in 120 ms and the task moves to Done". Use for interaction design.
- The product's job: "drag tasks onto days and see hours left per day". Use for apps.
- The list of care details: "undo on every action, drafts saved every 5 seconds". Use for quality claims.
- Cut it in product UI; users do not need to be told how to feel.
sleek
- Dimensions and material: "14 mm thick, aluminum, 1.2 kg". Use for hardware.
- What the kit contains: "48 components, light and dark themes, Figma and React". Use for UI kits.
- The design decision: "no visible screws; one USB-C port on the back". Use for reviews.
- Cut it when a measurement is in the sentence.
elegant
- The code property: "3 nested loops replaced by one dictionary lookup, 40 lines to 12". Use for code.
- The font specs: "high-contrast serif, 6 weights, small caps and old-style figures". Use for type.
- The readability rule it meets: "each function under 20 lines, no shared mutable state". Use for review comments.
- Cut it when you mean "I like it", and say what to keep.
modern
- The design spec: "IBM Plex Sans at 16 px, 2px radius, one accent #B4441C, borders not shadows". Use for design prompts.
- The named stack and versions: "React 19, Vite 6, Postgres 17". Use for READMEs.
- The audience and the job: "invoicing for freelancers who bill by the hour". Use for hero lines.
- Cut it every time; the word is never the claim.
next-generation
- The difference from the last version: "inspects TLS traffic at 10 Gbps; version 3 managed 2". Use for upgrades.
- The capability: "query events with SQL within 5 seconds of arrival". Use for analytics.
- The change in method: "plans in 2-week budgets, not dated milestones". Use for new product categories.
- Cut it in headings and name the product.
next-gen
- The rendering spec: "ray-traced shadows at 60 fps on a 2022 laptop GPU". Use for graphics.
- The mechanism and cost: "trades settle on-chain in about 12 seconds, fees under 0.01 USD". Use for finance.
- The feature the old tool lacks: "runs tests in parallel and skips unchanged files". Use for CLIs.
- Cut it in all cases; no reader needs it.
state-of-the-art
- The benchmark, score and date: "81.2 on MMLU, 1.4 points above the best published result as of March 2025". Use for ML.
- The named equipment: "a 3 tesla MRI scanner installed in 2024". Use for facilities.
- The controls: "authenticator app or hardware key; SOC 2 Type II report on request". Use for security.
- Cut it when you have no comparison to show.
world-class
- Credentials: "two Postgres committers and a former Rust compiler maintainer". Use for teams.
- The service terms: "phone support 24 hours a day, median wait 40 seconds". Use for support.
- The outside rating: "one Michelin star since 2019". Use only for ratings that exist.
- Cut it when no ranking stands behind it.
best-in-class
- The certification list: "SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, HIPAA BAA on request". Use for compliance.
- The service figure: "94% of 12,000 tickets rated resolved in 2024". Use for support claims.
- The benchmark with rivals named and the method linked. Use for performance.
- Cut it in RFP answers; procurement staff score evidence, not adjectives.
industry-leading
- The figure and the promise: "99.99% uptime in 2024 against a 99.9% SLA". Use for availability.
- The market share with its source: "used by 31% of US hospitals with over 500 beds". Use for position.
- What the AI does and how often it works: "agents send 55% of drafted replies unedited". Use for AI features.
- Cut it in press releases; journalists delete it anyway.
enterprise-grade
- The checklist items: "SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, audit log export, EU data residency". Use for security and admin.
- The contract terms: "99.9% SLA with service credits, 1-hour response for severity 1". Use for support.
- The limits: "up to 50,000 users per workspace". Use for scale.
- Cut it when the plan table already lists the features.
mission-critical
- The recovery targets: "recovery point 5 minutes, recovery time 30 minutes". Use for architecture docs.
- The cost of downtime: "the 3-hour outage in March delayed 120 quotes". Use for business cases.
- The tier and its response: "Tier 1 pages the on-call engineer within 60 seconds". Use for incident policy.
- Cut it when the sentence already says "production".
powerful
- What it does that a smaller tool does not: "validates nested JSON and reports every error with its path". Use for libraries.
- The specific feature: "a follow-up email after 3 days without a reply". Use for feature grids.
- The question it answers: "which 10 customers are most likely to cancel next month". Use for analytics.
- Cut it in pairs with "simple".
bleeding-edge
- The release channel and its risk: "nightly builds from `main`, breaking changes about weekly". Use for release docs.
- The tech list with versions: "Rust, WebGPU, Postgres 17". Use for hiring.
- What the framework does by default: "renders on the server and streams HTML". Use for framework pages.
- Cut it when the reader would rather know the stability guarantee.
top-notch
- The service terms: "same-day callback, 2-year warranty on every repair". Use for small businesses.
- The vetting step: "each developer passed a 4-hour paid trial project". Use for staffing.
- The specific reply: "sorry the hinge broke; a replacement ships today". Use for review replies.
- Cut it everywhere; it carries nothing a reader can check.
premium
- The plan name, price and contents: "Pro, 8 USD a month: unlimited projects and version history". Use for pricing.
- The material: "18-gauge stainless steel, 3-ply base". Use for goods.
- What the template includes: "40 pages, print-ready bleeds, a style guide". Use for templates.
- Cut it when the price is visible, because the price already says it.
bespoke
- What is custom and what is reused: "a booking system built on our open-source scheduler". Use for agencies.
- The input that changes the output: "recommendations change with every order and return". Use for retail.
- The deliverable and its source data: "a 12-month channel plan from your last 2 years of sales". Use for consulting.
- Cut it when the work starts from a template; say "custom" only if it is.
tailored
- The input: "picks from what you played in the last 30 days". Use for recommendations.
- The parameters: "plans built from headcount, region and payroll provider". Use for services.
- The branch: "admins see team setup first; members see their first task". Use for onboarding.
- Cut it when everyone gets the same content.
immersive
- The format: "a 20-minute VR walk through Pompeii, narrated by a historian". Use for exhibits.
- The method: "after week 2, lessons are only in Spanish". Use for language courses.
- The page behavior: "photos fade in on scroll over 150 ms; nothing moves under reduced motion". Use for web pages, and consider removing the effect.
- Cut it when the page is just large photos.
engaging
- The format and length: "5 posts a week, each under 200 words with one chart". Use for content plans.
- The exercise count and feedback: "48 exercises that run in the browser". Use for courses.
- The speaker's record: "closed PyCon 2024; the recording has 80,000 views". Use for introductions.
- Cut it in briefs, and write the metric you will judge by.
impactful
- The client outcome: "claims settled in 4 days instead of 11". Use for agency and consulting work.
- The before and after for one project: "median purchase time from 4 minutes to 90 seconds". Use for reviews.
- The single change and its effect: "one button label, sign-ups up 9%". Use for experiment write-ups.
- Cut it in slide titles and put the result in the title.
actionable
- The action with its trigger: "when weekly usage halves, the account owner gets an alert". Use for analytics.
- The steps themselves: "keep the bedroom at 18 C; no screens 1 hour before bed". Use for tips.
- The owner and the date: "the platform team retires the v1 API by 30 June". Use for report recommendations.
- Cut it everywhere and write the action.
insightful
- The answer, with no preface. Use in chat replies.
- What you learned: "I had not seen the 2019 commute data; it changes my estimate". Use for comments and thanks.
- The book's argument and its evidence: "4-day weeks raise output in service jobs, data from 61 firms". Use for endorsements.
- Cut it as an opener every time.
thought-provoking
- The argument: "email, not meetings, takes most of a manager's week". Use for reviews.
- The disagreement: "the panel split 3 to 2 on banning phones in schools". Use for recaps.
- Who should read it and what it covers: "for engineers moving into management: hiring, firing, 1:1s". Use for roundups.
- Cut it when the next sentence states the argument.
empowering
- The new ability: "managers approve time off from their phone". Use for tools.
- The program details: "a 10-week paid apprenticeship; 70% of graduates got offers". Use for programs.
- The capability and who stays in control: "10 captioned clips from a 1-hour video; you pick which to post". Use for AI tools.
- Cut it in mission statements and name what people do with the product.
visionary
- The prediction and its date, when there was one: "In 2016 she moved the API to Lambda, two years before our competitors."
- The decision that turned out right, with what it cost at the time.
- The work the person did with their own hands: "She wrote the first version of the scheduler."
- Cut it when there is no prediction or decision behind it. The name and job title are enough.
pioneering
- The first, with a date and a source: "the first CDN to cache authenticated responses, in 2019 (per our launch post)".
- If it was not first, what it does differently: "caches per user instead of per URL".
- For research, the finding and its size: the sample, the effect, the year.
- Cut it when you cannot name who came second.
forward-thinking
- The plan and its horizon: "We publish a 12-month roadmap and update it each quarter."
- A decision made before it was required: "We required hardware keys for all staff in 2021."
- The partners by name, or their count and sector.
- Cut it when the noun after it carries the sentence alone.
ever-evolving
- The change and its date: "React 19 removed `defaultProps` for function components."
- The release cadence as a number: "We shipped 26 releases in 2025; the changelog lists each one."
- The new threat by name: "Phishing kits now relay MFA prompts in real time."
- Cut it when it opens a paragraph. Start with the second sentence.
ever-changing
- The need that changed, from what to what: "Customers now ask for weekly invoicing instead of monthly."
- The rule and its effective date: "The EU AI Act transparency duties apply from August 2026."
- The demand as a number: "Order volume triples in the last two weeks of November."
- Cut it when the sentence after it names the change anyway.
fast-paced
- Release cadence: "We deploy to production about 30 times a day."
- Hours and on-call: "One week of on-call every six weeks; core hours 10:00 to 16:00."
- Scope with team size: "Four engineers own payments, from the API to the ledger."
- Cut it when it describes an industry. Every industry describes itself this way.
myriad
- The count: "reads 14 formats".
- The list, if it is short: "CSV, Parquet and JSON Lines".
- The two that matter plus the count of the rest: "CSV, Parquet and 12 others (see the table)".
- Cut it when nothing follows it. Write the list or delete the sentence.
plethora
- The number and the kinds: "42 templates: 18 invoices, 12 reports, 12 letters".
- A choice rule instead of a count: which option to pick, and when.
- The metrics by name, three to five of them.
- Cut it when the number is small. "Six templates" is stronger than any plural adjective.
diverse
- The list or the count: "customers in logistics, retail and healthcare".
- For people, the dimension and the number: "40 people in 11 countries; 45 percent are women".
- For data, the composition: where it came from and in what shares.
- Cut it when it modifies "range". Write the range.
vast
- Size with units and rate: "4 TB a day, about 50,000 events per second".
- The count: "310 components".
- The ratio and the benchmark: "3.2x faster on TPC-H at scale factor 10".
- Cut it when the reader does not need the size at all.
boundless
- What the tool lets people do: the features, with counts.
- Two concrete uses: "Teams use it for storyboards and for print ads."
- The real cap: "2 TB per team; files up to 50 GB."
- Cut it when it ends a section. The section already ended.
limitless
- The quota and what happens at it: "100,000 calls a day; above that, requests return 429 until 00:00 UTC."
- "No cap on X" only when true, with the fair-use rule if one exists.
- The next step the reader can take, in place of a motivational line.
- Cut it when there is a limit. There always is one.
timeless
- The choices: "Headings in Source Serif 4 at 32/40px; body in IBM Plex Sans at 16px."
- The reason behind them: "an open license and active maintenance since 2014, so we never pay to relicense".
- The constraint you set: "two colors and one typeface, so the mark survives fax and embroidery".
- Cut it when the claim is about future taste.
iconic
- Recognition data, if you have it: "In a 2024 survey, 71 percent of US adults named the brand from the logo alone."
- Age and reach: "used since 1998, printed on 40 million boxes a year".
- For places, distance with units: "a 12-minute walk".
- Cut it when the name is famous. The name already does the work.
quintessential
- The traits that make it typical: "modal editing, a macro language, three decades of plugins".
- Observed details: what is on the counter, what it costs, when it opens.
- The scope of a guide: topics, length, number of examples.
- Cut it when the noun already names the category.
crisp
- For type, size, weight and contrast: "Body 16px IBM Plex Sans, #1A1A18 on #F7F5F0, 16:1."
- For icons, grid, stroke and format: "20px grid, 1.5px stroke, SVG, so edges stay sharp at 2x and 3x."
- For copy, the length rule: "Button labels two words at most; error messages under 80 characters."
- Cut it when nothing measurable follows it.
clean
- For design, what was removed and the rule that remains: "one accent color, 1px rules instead of cards, 24px between sections".
- For code, the measurable change: files split, lines removed, functions under a size limit, tests unchanged.
- For a review comment, the decision you approve and why it works.
- Cut it when the sentence praises without informing.
beautiful
- What the thing shows, and how long it takes: "Revenue, churn and runway on one page, from your Stripe data, in about 5 minutes."
- The design decisions: typeface, palette, smallest supported width.
- For review, the property that works: labels, axis, color use.
- Cut it when a screenshot sits next to the sentence. The screenshot is the evidence.
gorgeous
- The palette and contrast: background and text hex values, with the WCAG level every pair passes.
- What each template contains: pages, print styles, supported widths.
- The change and its measured effect.
- Cut it when the image is right next to the sentence.
slick
- Steps and time: "three screens, about 40 seconds, no email confirmation before first use".
- Motion values: duration, easing, properties animated, reduced-motion behavior.
- For decks, the rule: "one claim per slide, numbers set at 56px".
- Cut it when it is the whole review.
snappy
- Latency percentiles with the input size: "p95 from 640ms to 180ms on a 50,000-document index".
- Install size and memory: "12 MB download, 60 MB RAM at idle".
- For UI, the interaction spec: time to pressed state, duration, easing.
- Cut it when you have no number. Measure first.
blazing

- Page load metrics at a percentile, with the device and network.

- Search: index size and latency at a percentile.
- Deploys: median and p95 time from push to live.
- Support: the first-reply commitment, with hours and time zone.
- Cut it when the number is unflattering. Fix the speed, then publish the number.
buttery
- Frame data from a trace: fps, dropped frames, device, list length.
- The technique that produces it: "rows are virtualized; 40 are in the DOM at once".
- Motion limits: duration, properties animated, behavior on 60Hz and 120Hz screens.
- Cut it when you have not run a trace.
magical
- The mechanism in one sentence: what input produces what output.
- For loading states, what is happening and how long it takes.
- For docs, the rule, with one example mapping.
- Cut it when the sentence promises. Describe instead.
whimsical
- The illustration spec: line weight, colors, what is never drawn.
- Voice rules with limits: how many jokes, and where jokes are banned.
- The content the page needs: what happened and where to go next.
- Cut it when the copy is an error message. Errors need facts.
harmonious
- The palette rule and the contrast: neutrals in N steps, one accent, ratios against the background.
- What syncs between tools, in which direction, and how fast.
- Team practices a candidate can check in an interview.
- Cut it when it describes how people feel and you have not asked them.
synergistic
- What customers can now do that they could not before.
- How two features interact, with one example.
- The team change and a before-and-after number.
- Cut it when there is no combined effect to report yet.
cohesive
- The shared source: one token file, one icon set, one component library, and who reads them.
- For review comments, the exact inconsistency and the value to match.
- For brand, the places and the shared elements, listed.
- Cut it when you cannot point to a token or a rule.
sophisticated
- For incidents, the entry point, the date and the missing control.
- For algorithms, the method and the evaluation result on held-out data.
- For palettes, the hex values and their roles.
- Cut it when you cannot name a single thing that makes it advanced.
granular
- The unit of control and the levels: "per project and per environment: view, deploy, admin".
- The unit of data and the retention: "per session, kept 13 months".
- For logging, the fields and the trigger.
- Cut it when "per X" says it in fewer words.
nimble
- Cycle time: "median 6 days from approved design to production".
- The decision path: who approves a change, and how many people that is.
- The architecture fact that allows change: independent deploys, isolated schemas.
- Cut it when the claim is about a market. Say what you will change, and when.
proactive
- The trigger and the response: which metric, which threshold, who responds, how fast.
- The behavior you expect from the hire, in one sentence.
- The controls and their deadlines.
- Cut it when "before" plus the event says it plainly.
strategic
- What the partnership changes for customers, and from when.
- The goal as a number, then the work aimed at it.
- For layout, the placement rule and its reason.
- Cut it when "plan", "goal" or nothing at all fits.

- Say what the point means for the reader.
- State the fact and drop the preamble.
- Cut it when `It's noteworthy that` comes before a statement. Delete those four words.
