- The thing done and its effect: what changed, and what it caught or saved.
- For a review with requests, the requests themselves, numbered, with no grade in front.
- For incidents, the timeline: detection, rollback, communication.
- For praise you mean, the reason it matters to the next person who reads the code.
- Cut it when it softens criticism. State the change you need.
exquisite
- The details, as specs: grid, alignment checks, export sizes.
- For food and hospitality, what is served, where it comes from, and the price.
- For type, the typeface, sizes, tracking and figure style.
- Cut it when the details follow anyway. Let them stand alone.
impeccable
- The rate and the period: "46 of 48 projects shipped on the contract date since 2019".
- Service numbers with sample size: satisfaction score, ticket count, year.
- For design, the rule and the audit result.
- Cut it when you cannot show the record.
flawless
- Migration facts: data moved, time taken, data lost, downtime, how you verified.
- The test matrix: OS versions, browsers, oldest device.
- For checkout, step count and payment error rate.
- Cut it when there were problems. Report them.
stellar
- Results with a baseline and a period.
- In thanks, name the specific thing and how it was used.
- For events, names, topics and session lengths.
- In a performance review, the outcome and the date: "Led the March outage review; the three fixes shipped by April."
- Cut it when the thanks would read better as a specific sentence anyway.
phenomenal
- Growth with start, end and period: "from 120 to 410 paying teams in 2025".
- Community numbers: stars, pull requests, new contributors, in a stated week.
- The benchmark, before and after, with the workload.
- When the number is small, the number anyway, with the trend: "Up from 40 to 55 teams, our best quarter so far."
- Cut it when the number speaks. It usually does.
epic
- The scope and length: word count, topics, diagrams.
- For a launch, what ships and on which date.
- In review, the effect of the change.
- For a big piece of work, its size: files touched, weeks spent, people involved.
- Cut it when the title already says "guide". Add the scope instead.
mind-blowing
- The result with the before and after numbers.
- What is new, in one plain sentence.
- In a list title, the count and the benefit: "10 VS Code shortcuts for multi-cursor editing".
- For a demo, the input and the output side by side, with the time it took.
- Cut it when the content follows. The content does better unannounced.
steadfast
- The policy terms: what you do not do, retention periods, audits.
- Contract terms and tenure: price locks, median customer lifetime.
- For a person, what they did and for how long.
- For a company stance, the date it was taken and one case where it cost you something.
- Cut it when the terms are on the page anyway.
enduring
- The age and the evidence: founding year, what still works.
- Customer tenure as a number.
- The principles, each with what it rules out.
- For a product, the support period in writing: "Security updates until at least 2031."
- Cut it when it closes a paragraph. The paragraph is done.
adept
- Evidence of the skill: one project, who was involved, the result.
- One problem solved, with numbers.
- For a model, the eval: test set, size, score, who graded.
- Cut it when the evidence follows. Lead with the evidence.
disruptive
- The incumbent and the difference, in time or price.
- What the technology does, in one sentence.
- The pricing facts beside the usual price.
- Cut it when you cannot name the incumbent.
ai-powered
- What the feature outputs, when, and for whom.
- What it does to the user's text, and who approves each change.
- How the behavior differs from keyword matching, with one example.
- When the model matters, which one and where the data goes.
ai-driven
- What the model does and what the human does, in that order.
- The decision volume and the override rate.
- For personalization, the input, the output and what data stays where.
- Cut it when a person makes the final call. Say that instead.
data-driven
- One decision and the data behind it.
- The metric you track and its target.
- For design, the test: variants, sample size, result.
- Cut it when there is no decision to cite.
customer-centric
- The policy a customer can use: refunds, cancellations, who may approve them.
- The practice that keeps staff in contact with customers, with numbers.
- Support terms: channels, hours, response time.
- Cut it when the policy is on the page. Show the policy.
user-centric
- The research: method, number of sessions, who took part.
- The decision the research changed: "Testing showed users looked for export under Reports, so we moved it there."
- For a screen, who it is for and the task it serves.
- The process as steps with counts and durations.
- Cut it when you did no research. Say what you did instead.
human-centric
- The controls users keep: drafts, approvals, opt-outs.
- What the automation does and which tasks stay with people.
- For spaces, the specifics: light, quiet rooms per head, desk options.
- Cut it when there is no control to list.
mission-driven
- The mission as an outcome for a named group of people.
- Evidence of progress: how many people, how much, since when.
- Pay and terms, since readers suspect the word replaces them.
- Cut it when the mission sentence is on the page. That sentence is enough.
purpose-driven
- The purpose and the measured result.
- For leadership, one decision that cost money and why it was made.
- Supply chain facts: where, who audits, how often.
- Cut it when you cannot attach a number.
turnkey
- Setup steps and typical time.
- The integrations by name and what each one syncs.
- What the customer still has to provide.
- Cut it when the setup steps are listed. They make the claim better.
plug-and-play
- The install command and the minimum configuration, as code.
- Compatibility: framework versions, dependencies, size.
- For hiring, what the person must already know, and when they start on-call.
- For hardware add-ons, the ports, drivers and operating systems supported.
- Cut it when you can show the three lines of setup. Show them.
battle-tested
- The production record: since when, how much traffic, at whom.
- Adoption with a source: download counts, an adopters file.
- For a process, the safeguards and how often they fired.
- Cut it when you have no production record yet. Say it is new.
end-to-end
- The stages covered, and the ones you leave to the customer.
- The support scope, from first step to last, with durations.
- What is tracked, between which points, and how often it updates.
- Cut it when you list the stages. The list is the claim.
all-in-one
- The tools it replaces, by category.
- The feature list with what it leaves out.
- One price and what it includes.
- Cut it when the feature list is shown. Name the gap instead.
one-stop
- The catalog with counts and the license.
- For docs, what is covered and how it is searched.
- For services, the stages you handle, and the ones you do not.
- Cut it when the counts are on the page.
unified
- What is combined and how the parts link.
- Which sources feed the view and the match key.
- For design, the shared files and the apps that use them.
- Cut it when "one" says it: one query language, one login, one token file.
curated
- Who chose, and the rule they used.
- For newsletters, the count, the day and the editor.
- For shops, the selection criteria a buyer can check.
- Cut it when "picked by" plus a name says it better.
handcrafted
- What the kit contains, as counts and features.
- For code, who wrote and reviewed it, and what is generated.
- For physical goods, the maker, the place and the steps done by hand.
- Cut it when the product is software. Describe its contents.
nestled
- Location with altitude, distance and travel time.
- Address area and transit time.
- For layout, position, alignment, width and gap.
- Cut it when the location follows. "In" works.
tapestry
- The parts, with numbers.
- For a codebase or a team, the components and who owns each one.
- The features and how one feeds the next.
- The career in order, with years.
- Cut it when the list follows. Keep the list.
testament
- Who did what, with time spent.
- The cause you can show, with its mechanism.
- The rating with its count and source.
- For a person's character, an event that shows it, with the date.
- Cut it when it closes a paragraph. The fact before it is enough.
realm
- The field name alone, or the specific subtopic.
- The possibility, named: what a user can now do.
- The topic and the scope of the piece.
- For docs, the product area by its menu name: "Settings, Billing".
- Cut it when it opens the sentence. Start with the claim.
landscape
- The competitors by name, with their position.
- The specific change, with dates.
- The list of options and the criteria used to compare them.
- Cut it when the list follows. Start with the list.
journey
- For a course, length, weekly hours and what the learner builds.
- For UX, the flow: steps, and where people drop off.
- For thanks, what the people did and how many of them.
- For a career story, the jobs in order with years.
- Cut it when the steps are known. Write the steps.
odyssey
- "migration", "rewrite", "project" when the thing is a piece of work with a scope.
- A date range ("from March to June 2024") when the length is the point.
- "history" when the text walks through past events in order.
- Cut it when the sentence works with the plain noun alone; "our move to microservices" says the same thing.
symphony
- For systems, name the parts and the order they run in: "the scheduler enqueues a job, a worker picks it up within 2 s".
- For food, name the ingredients.
- "together" or "in sequence" when a short connector is enough.
- Cut it when the sentence is only there to sound pleasant; the list of parts already says they combine.
beacon
- The record that earns the praise: "99.98% uptime over 24 months".
- "example" or "model" when the point is that others should copy it.
- What the person did, with numbers: "mentored 40 engineers", "founded the meetup".
- Cut it when the claim has no evidence behind it; delete the sentence.
cornerstone
- "first rule" or "main reason" when the claim is about priority, then say what it outranks.
- The concrete practice: "every PR needs a passing type check".
- "depends on" when you mean dependency: "every report depends on this table".
- Cut it when the sentence states a value with no practice behind it.
linchpin
- "single point of failure" when losing the part takes the system down, which is often the more honest framing.
- "depends on", with the dependent parts named.
- What the person did, as a list of results.
- Cut it when the claim is a slogan with no data under it.
bedrock
- "runs on" or "is built on" for software layers, with the version.
- "base layer" when you describe a stack diagram.
- The behavior that shows the value, for people and teams.
- Cut it when the sentence is a value statement no reader would dispute.
catalyst
- "led to", "caused", "started", with the result named.
- "after" plus a date when you can show only sequence, not cause.
- "reason" when the sentence explains a decision.
- Cut it when the change or growth has no number or description.
paradigm
- "approach", "model" or "way" when the plain noun does the job.
- A before and after pair: "before, X; now, Y".
- "style" for programming style: "functional style", "declarative style".
- Cut it when the sentence says only that the thing is new.
synergy
- The saving or gain in numbers: "cuts $2M a year in duplicate licenses".
- "work together" or "share", plus what is shared.
- "overlap" when the two groups do some of the same work.
- Cut it when there is no measured gain; write what each part does instead.
ecosystem
- "packages", "plugins" or "integrations" with a count: "over 2,000 plugins on npm".
- "community" only if you can say how many people and where they meet.
- The 3 to 5 most used items, named, instead of a description of the set.
- Cut it when the sentence is about size alone and you lack the number.
nexus
- "where X and Y meet", only if both things are real and named.
- "hub" or "center" with a number: "home to 300 AI startups".
- What the thing does: "pulls data from 6 sources into one view".
- Cut it when it is only positioning; a bio can list jobs instead.
crucible
- "hard", "difficult" or "under pressure", followed by what ran out or what broke.
- "test" when you mean a period that showed what worked.
- The lesson, in one sentence.
- Cut it when the hard period has no cause or outcome you can state.
mosaic
- The composition: "people from 14 countries who speak 11 languages".
- "mix" or "range", with the items named.
- A plain list of the actual items.
- Cut it when the sentence praises variety without naming any members.
kaleidoscope
- The actual colors, as names or hex values.
- "many" or "several", with a count.
- Two or three specific items, named.
- Cut it when the sentence exists to add color to the prose rather than information.
labyrinth
- "complicated" or "hard to follow", plus the reason.
- The count of steps, files or menus.
- "maze" is shorter but has the same problem; prefer the count.
- Cut it when the following sentences already describe the problem.
treasure trove
- "collection", "archive" or "set", with the count and the topic.
- The 2 or 3 entries most readers need, named.
- "reference" for docs that people look things up in.
- Cut it when the link text and the item name already make the case.
game-changer
- The measured change: "cut review time from 2 days to 4 hours".
- "big improvement", only when the number follows.
- A description of the feature, so the reader can judge.
- Cut it when there is no number; the feature description is enough.
powerhouse
- The spec or benchmark: cores, GB, ms, requests per second.
- "large", "fast" or "productive", followed by the number that proves it.
- What the person shipped or grew.
- Cut it when the noun already carries the meaning and the benchmark follows.
juggernaut
- The company name plus a number and a source.
- "largest" or "market leader" when rank is the point, with the source.
- "widely used", plus a survey figure.
- Cut it when the company name alone tells the reader its size.
trailblazer
- The first thing and its date: "wrote the A-0 compiler in 1952".
- "early" or "first", with the evidence.
- "founder" or the job title.
- Cut it when you cannot name what came first.
frontier
- "new area", "open problem" or "early stage", with what remains unsolved.
- "next step" when it is a roadmap item.
- The current limit as a number: "cold start is still 300 ms".
- Cut it when the sentence is only about being early.
interplay
- The relation as a cause: "text at 24px and up needs 3:1 contrast instead of 4.5:1".
- "how X affects Y", one direction at a time.
- "trade-off" when gaining one costs the other.
- Cut it when the article then treats X and Y separately anyway.
intricacies
- "details", "rules" or "edge cases", then list them.
- "how X works" for the intro of an explanation.
- The 2 or 3 hard parts, named.
- Cut it when the following sections already cover the details.
complexities
- Each hard part, named: "currency conversion, local tax and 3-day settlement".
- "problems", "steps" or "rules", with a count.
- "complexity" in the singular, only for a measured property: "O(n log n) time complexity", "cyclomatic complexity of 14".
- Cut it when the sentence says only that a topic is hard.
insight
- "finding" or "result" for a research outcome, then state it.
- The metric itself: "churn by plan", "days from signup to first purchase".
- "report", "chart" or "alert" for what the product shows.
- Cut it when the next sentence states the finding; start with that sentence.
takeaway
- "Summary" as a heading, if a summary is needed at all.
- "Next steps" when the list is actions.
- "Lessons" or "conclusions", with each one stated as a full claim.
- Cut it when the article is short enough that a recap repeats the body, which is most articles.
superpower
- "skill", "advantage" or "habit", plus what it lets the reader do.
- The time saved or the task now possible.
- The feature described directly: "search 2 million files in under a second".
- Cut it when the sentence is only encouragement.
secret sauce
- "advantage", "difference" or "method", then describe it.
- What the method does, at whatever detail you can disclose.
- If you cannot disclose it, say so: "the ranking model is not public".
- Cut it when nothing secret exists; the phrase makes readers look for it.
north star
- "main goal" or "top goal", with the target and the date.
- "primary metric" for the one number a team is judged on.
- A rule people can apply: "if a design fails WCAG AA, it does not ship".
- Cut it when the goal has no number or rule attached.
moonshot
- "long-shot project" or "high-risk project" when risk is the point, with the odds if known.
- The goal as a number with a date.
- "research project" for work with no product yet.
- Cut it when the sentence is only about ambition.
holy grail
- "hard goal" or "long-standing goal", with why it is hard.
- The existing approaches and their limits.
- "ideal" for a target state, followed by how close you are.
- Cut it when the topic is a known technique with documentation.
silver bullet
- "no single fix", then the 2 or 3 fixes that do help.
- The trade-off: "microservices add network calls and deploy overhead".
- For a product claim, the measured result on a stated workload.
- Cut it when the hedge closes a paragraph that already listed the options.
low-hanging fruit
- "quick fixes" or "easy changes", with time estimates.
- A table with the change, the effort in hours and the expected gain.
- "Start with", plus the item and its numbers.
- Cut it when the list that follows already shows effort and gain.
best practices
- The rule itself: "parameterize every SQL query".
- The source: "meets WCAG 2.2 AA", "passes OWASP ASVS level 2".
- "conventions" for team or language norms, with a link.
- Cut it when the list that follows states the rules.
thought leader
- The person's job and work: "head of design at X, author of Y".
- "expert", only with the evidence next to it: books, papers, systems built.
- "speaker" for event lineups, with the talk title.
- Cut it when the bio already lists the work.
thought leadership
- The format: "essay", "report", "research", "talk".
- The topic and the data source.
- "articles by our staff" for a company blog.
- Cut it when the title of the piece already tells the reader what it is.
value proposition
- The offer: what the customer gets, at what price, in how much time.
- "why customers buy" in internal docs, followed by the reasons heard on sales calls.
- "offer" or "pitch" when you need a noun.
- Cut it when the next sentence states the offer.
bandwidth
- "time", with hours: "I have 4 free hours this week".
- "capacity" for teams, with headcount or points.
- A plain "no" or "not before", with a date.
- Cut it when the refusal works without a reason.
touchpoint
- The channel and the moment: "the welcome email", "the cancel screen", "the renewal call".
- "step" for a flow, numbered.
- "contact" for support conversations.
- Cut it when the list of screens or emails already exists.
narrative
- "story" for a sequence of events.
- "explanation", "account" or "message", with the content stated.
- "the common view that", followed by the view.
- Cut it when you can write the claims themselves.
storytelling
- "explain", "show" or "write", plus the object.
- For charts, the one finding the chart must show, placed in its title.
- "sequence" or "order of steps" for onboarding.
- Cut it when the method described is just writing.
passion
- What the person or team has done that shows care: hours, projects, details.
- "interest" or "focus" when a neutral noun is needed.
- "I like" or "I care about" in personal writing, followed by an example.
- Cut it when the sentence states a feeling and nothing else.
endeavor
- "try" or "aim" for the verb, and drop it entirely when you can promise.
- "project", "work" or "job" for the noun.
- The next thing, named: "good luck at the clinic".
- Cut it when the sentence is a sign-off; end the email on the last useful line.
harmony
- The rule: "one accent color, used only for primary actions".
- "consistent", with what is consistent: the spacing scale, the type scale.
- "works with", plus the named tools.
- Cut it when the sentence is about mood; state the policy instead.
essence
- The property: "the logo is a single line drawing of a bridge".
- "main point" or "core idea" when summarizing, then the idea itself.
- The features that make it typical: ingredients, methods, materials.
- Cut it when the next sentence states the property; start there.
forefront
- The evidence: what you did first, papers, patents, market share.
- "led" or "first", with the date.
- "made common" or "made visible" for the "bring to" form.
- Cut it when there is no evidence of rank.
cusp
- "about to" or "close to", with the date or the gap.
- The current number and the threshold: "$40k a month short of break-even".
- "expected in", plus a quarter and a source.
- Cut it when there is no date or number; the claim is a guess.
crossroads
- "has to choose between X and Y", with both options named.
- "decision", plus the date it must be made.
- A table of the options with their costs.
- Cut it when the following paragraph lists the options; start there.
underpinning
- "basis", "theory" or "foundations" for ideas, then name them.
- "runs on" or "is built from" for systems, with the component list.
- "causes" or "reasons" for behavior.
- Cut it when the next sentence names the theory.
arsenal
- "toolkit" or "set of tools", only with the list.
- The tools, named, with what each does.
- "features", with a count.
- Cut it when the noun before it already says what the thing is.
blueprint
- "plan", "template", "checklist" or "guide", whichever it is.
- "spec" or "design doc" in engineering.
- The steps themselves.
- Cut it when the title can name the content.
solution
- The product type: "app", "API", "database", "service", "plugin".
- "fix", "answer" or "workaround" in support and code answers.
- "way" when you mean a method: "one way to do this is".
- Cut it when the code or steps follow directly; start with them.
innovation
- The new thing, named: product, method or patent, with a date.
- "new", "first" or "change" when a plain word works.
- "research" for R&D, with the budget or headcount.
- Cut it when the sentence contains no new thing.
engagement
- The action counted: "daily active users", "replies per post", "sessions per week".
- "use" or "activity" in a general sense, with the metric next to it.
- For staff surveys, the questions or the score.
- Cut it when there is no metric; the sentence is a slogan.
delight
- The task outcome: "the export finishes in 3 seconds".
- "pleased", "glad" or "happy" in personal messages, when the feeling is real.
- The detail users notice: "the form keeps your input after an error".
- Cut it when the sentence promises the reader a feeling.
magic
- What happens, step by step: "we detect column types, then match them to your fields".
- "automatically", with what is automatic.
- The function or model, named, with its limits.
- Cut it when the next sentence explains the mechanism.
wow factor
- The feature that draws attention: the size, the material, the result shown.
- "first impression" when that is the point, with what the viewer sees in the first 5 seconds.
- For demos, the result the buyer wants, shown with real data.
- Cut it when the advice would add decoration; drop the effect as well.
prowess
- "skill", plus the evidence.
- The result: release count, defect rate, awards.
- The specific craft: "she cures her own ham".
- Cut it when the evidence is already in the next sentence.
excellence
- The standard: "every PR gets two reviews", "99.9% uptime".
- "quality", with a measure next to it.
- For team names, what the team does: "the platform team", "the design systems group".
- Cut it when the sentence is a value with no standard.
transformation
- "migration", "rewrite", "redesign" or "reorganization", whichever it was.
- Before and after numbers.
- "change" when a plain noun is enough.
- Cut it when the sentence only announces change; list the changes.
masterpiece
- The qualities, named: precision, materials, measured performance.
- "well made" or "good", with the reason.
- In code review, the specific change you liked and why.
- Cut it when the praise has no reason.
vibe
- The properties: palette hex values, typeface, spacing, corner radius.
- "mood" or "tone" in a brief, followed by those specifics.
- For code, how it was made and checked: "generated with an assistant, not reviewed, no tests".
- Cut it when the sentence describes only a feeling.
furthermore
- Start with the claim: "The API supports pagination."
- "and" or "also" inside the sentence when the two points belong together.
- A bulleted list when you have 3 or more parallel points.
- Cut it when the next sentence plainly adds to the last; the reader already knows it is an addition.
moreover
- Start the sentence with the claim; its position already marks it as the next point.
- "also" for a point of similar weight: "The plan also includes support."
- "and" to join two short claims in one sentence.
- Cut it when the connective is propping up a weak point; drop the point too.
additionally
- "also" in the middle of the sentence: "You can also export reports as PDF."
- One bulleted list, when there are 3 or more items.
- "and" to join two related facts.
- Cut it when the sentence starts a new paragraph; the break already signals a new point.
notably
- "including" or "such as" for examples.
- Why it matters: "the cache halves p95 latency".
- The most important item placed first, with no adverb.
- Cut it when the sentence works without it, which is nearly always.
importantly
- The consequence: "the upgrade deletes the old index, so back up first".
- The most important point placed first in the paragraph or list.
- A warning callout in docs, with the failure stated.
- Cut it when the point is not the most important one, which is most of the time.
crucially
- The failure: "if you call it after render, the first frame shows unstyled text".
- "because", to show why the fact matters.
- The condition placed in a numbered step or a warning.
- Cut it when the fact carries its own weight.
ultimately
- The verdict, with its condition: "pick Vue if your team knows templates; pick React if you need React Native".
- "in the end" or "finally", only for order in time.
- A tie-breaker rule when the options are close.
- Cut it when the sentence works without it, which it nearly always does; delete sentences that hand the choice back.
essentially
- The full definition, including the edge that the adverb skipped.
- "nearly" or "the same except", with the difference named.
- "basically" has the same problem; do not swap one for the other.
- Cut it when the sentence restates the last one; delete the restatement.
fundamentally
- A direct definition with a verb that does work: "renders", "stores", "blocks". Use it when the sentence defines a thing.
- The cause, named: "The cause was X." Use it when you separate a symptom from its source.
- A number that shows the tradeoff, when the sentence claims one.
- Cut it when the sentence stays true without it, which is nearly always.
arguably
- The evidence for the ranking: a benchmark, a download count, a survey with its year.
- "I think" or "We picked X because" when the claim is an opinion and the reader should know whose.
- A narrower true claim in place of the superlative: "the only one of the three with X".
- Cut it when you cannot name the argument; then the ranking goes too.
undeniably
- The measurement: "Load time fell from 2.4s to 1.1s."
- The source: "The 2025 Stack Overflow survey puts TypeScript at 38%."
- A scoped claim: "On our team" or "in the 14 interviews we ran".
- Cut it when the fact is plain; a plain fact needs no guard.
undoubtedly
- A forecast with its basis: "Based on the pilot, we expect X."
- A measured past result in place of a future promise.
- The specific qualification for a person: years, projects, outcomes.
- Cut it when the sentence is a prediction you cannot support; cut the prediction too.
indeed
- "Yes" when you are answering a question.
- The evidence itself, with no confirming word before it.
- "In fact" only when you correct a wrong belief, and say what the belief was.
- Cut it when the sentence before already made the point.
truly
- The number behind "scale": requests per second, tenants, rows.
- A specific thanks that names what the person did.
- The one property that differs from the usual approach, named.
- Cut it when the adjective after it can stand alone; if it cannot, replace the adjective.
genuinely
- The use: what task the tool does and for whom.
- An acknowledgment of the cost to the user, followed by the fix.
- The specific page or section that helped.
- Cut it when the sentence carries a claim; the claim is enough.
incredibly
- The measured value with its baseline: "builds in 4s, down from 38s".
- A count of steps or minutes for ease.
- The work itself, listed, in place of "busy".
- Cut it when there is no number; then cut the claim it was propping up.
remarkably
- The expectation and the result: "We expected a 5% drop; errors fell 60%."
- The integration measured in lines of code or calls.
- The score and the benchmark name.
- Cut it when there was no expectation to break.
profoundly
- The before and after, each stated: "In 2010 we did X. Now we do Y."
- Who is affected, how many, and in what way.
- The specific idea you took from the book and where you applied it.
- Cut it when the verb after it is abstract; replace the verb.
inherently
- The mechanism: what makes it so, in one clause starting with "because".
- The specific failure mode the property causes.
- A condition: "when X" or "unless Y", if the property depends on setup.
- Cut it when the reason follows; the reason carries the claim.
invariably
- A frequency with its sample: "in 9 of our last 12 incidents".
- "Always" when it is a rule of the system, and name the rule.
- "Often" or "usually" with an example, when you have no count.
- Cut it when the claim works as a tendency; most claims do.
interestingly
- The expectation it breaks: "We expected X; we saw Y."
- A causal link: "because", "so", or "which means".
- The fact alone, with its numbers, so the reader judges it.
- Cut it when nothing was expected; the fact stands without a frame.
overall
- The result with its measure: "The migration finished in 4 hours with no downtime."
- The specific parts that changed, by name.
- The exceptions first, since they are the news.
- Cut it when the paragraph already made the point.
thereby
- Two sentences: the action, then the effect with its number.
- "so" between the clauses when the effect is short.
- The effect alone, if the action is obvious from context.
- Cut it when the consequence is a vague benefit; state the measured one or drop it.
whereby
- An active sentence with the actor as subject: "The gateway assigns each request an ID."
- "in which" or "where" if you must keep the clause.
- A numbered list when the process has steps.
- Cut it when the noun before it ("system", "process") adds nothing.
albeit
- "but" followed by the specific limitation.
- Two sentences when the limitation matters as much as the claim.
- The number, when "slightly" is the concession.
- Cut it when the concession is vague; name it or delete it.
aforementioned
- The noun again: "`initTheme()`", "the timeout issue".
- "this" or "that" when the referent is in the previous sentence.
- A link to the section, when the referent is far away.
- Cut it when "the" alone points clearly enough.
in conclusion
- Nothing. End on the last new fact or the last step.
- A decision or recommendation, stated as the final line: "Use Postgres unless you need X."
- A summary at the top (TL;DR) instead of the bottom, for long documents.
- Cut it when the final paragraph only restates; cut the paragraph too.
in summary
- The answer in the first sentence, so no summary is needed.
- A TL;DR line at the top of long pages.
- A list of the specific changes requested, for reviews.
- Cut it when the body is under a screen long.
to summarize
- The steps as a numbered list, once, with no prose recap.
- The specific change, measured.
- Decisions and owners, for meeting notes: "Decision: X. Owner: Ana. Date: 20 Oct."
- Cut it when the summary would repeat the last 5 lines.
all in all
- The verdict with the deciding factor: "Svelte, because the bundle is 40% smaller."
- The result against the goal: "We aimed for 500 signups and got 820."
- The one thing that tipped the decision.
- Cut it when the verdict is already clear from the text above.
at its core
- The definition, starting with the subject and a concrete verb.
- The one action the product performs, for whom.
- The specific design rule, stated as a rule.
- Cut it when what follows is a definition; definitions need no frame.
at the end of the day
- The specific priority that wins, and what it beats: "We fix the crash before the redesign."
- The decision rule: "If X, choose A."
- Nothing, when the line is a platitude.
- Cut it when the sentence after it could close any article.
needless to say
- The fact alone.
- An instruction with its reason, when the fact is a warning.
- The result with its number, for reactions.
- Cut it every time; the phrase never carries meaning.
worth noting
- The fact, stated where it applies.
- A labeled warning block in docs ("Warning" or "Note") when the reader must not miss it.
- The fact moved to the first line, if it changes the answer.
- Cut it when the clause after it can stand alone, which is always.
important to note
- A warning placed before the step it affects, in its own block.
- The specific condition, in place of "results may vary".
- The fact stated in the step where the reader needs it.
- Cut it when the fact is not a risk; put it in the body.
in today's
- The specific fact with its date: "In 2026, 70% of our traffic is mobile."
- The problem the reader has, in their terms.
- Nothing; start with the second sentence.
- Cut it when the sentence would be equally true in 2005.
digital age
- The specific technology and the year it changed things.
- The specific adaptation: "Libraries now lend e-books through Libby."
- The service you provide, named.
- Cut it when the claim holds without a time frame.
digital landscape
- The market, named: "B2B payroll software in the UK".
- The specific change, with its date: "Google moved to mobile-first indexing in 2019."
- The channels you work in: search, email, App Store.
- Cut it when you cannot name the market; the sentence has nothing to say.
let's dive
- The first step, as a heading or an imperative: "Install the CLI."
- A one-line scope at the top: "This guide covers setup and the first deploy."
- Nothing; delete the introduction it closes.
- Cut it when the next line is the content; it always is.
buckle up
- The length and scope: "This post is 3,000 words and covers 5 layout methods."
- The first point.
- A table of contents for long pieces.
- Cut it when there is no seatbelt.
next level
- The skill or result the reader will have afterward.
- The measured change.
- The tool's job, named.
- Cut it when there is no defined level; there never is.
the power of
- The task the tool does: "drafts replies to support tickets".
- The specific benefit in a large codebase: "renames across 400 files".
- What two people can do at once, named.
- Cut it when the noun alone carries the meaning.
at the forefront
- The first or only thing you did, with its date.
- A count: papers, patents, customers, years.
- The specific research question and the result.
- Cut it when you have no evidence of being first.
on the cusp
- The date or the condition: "ships in March", "after the FDA review".
- The current status, named: "in private beta with 40 users".
- The specific result so far, with its number.
- Cut it when there is no date and no status; then there is no news.
pave the way
- "lets us" or "unblocks" followed by the named next step.
- "is required for" when the change is a prerequisite.
- The specific later result and the link between the two.
- Cut it when the future step is not planned; describe the change on its own terms.
bridge the gap
- The mechanism: what moves from one side to the other, and how.
- The specific thing learners do, for courses.
- The action either party takes, named.
- Cut it when you cannot name what crosses the gap.
stand out from the crowd
- The specific difference, named: what you have that the others do not.
- The outcome with a number: interview rate, click rate.
- The concrete service step.
- Cut it when the difference is not stated in the same sentence.
cut through the noise
- The filter rule: what is shown and what is hidden.
- The count: "5 links a week", "one alert per incident".
- The source and the selection method.
- Cut it when there is no stated rule.
ahead of the curve
- What the reader learns, and how soon after it happens.
- The specific early move a client made, with its date.
- The concrete feature the framework has that others lack.
- Cut it when there is no date; "ahead" needs a time to be ahead of.
push the boundaries
- The specific limit and the new value: "a 3D scene in 60 KB of JavaScript".
- What was done that others had not done, with a source.
- A number for performance.
- Cut it when the work is good but not new; say what it is.
outside the box
- The unusual idea, stated: what was tried that is not the default.
- The kind of problem candidates will solve, with an example.
- The exercise the workshop runs.
- Cut it when no unusual idea follows.
a wide range of
- The count and the top items: "42 formats, including PDF, DOCX, and HEIC".
- The full list, if it is under 8 items.
- The two or three industries with the most work, and the project count.
- Cut it when the list follows; the list proves the range.
a wide array of
- The specific options a user will look for first: colors, fonts, layout.
- A count with a link to the full list.
- The three helpers most people need, by name.
- Cut it when the next sentence lists the items.
look no further
- The offer, stated in the first sentence: who you are, what you do, where.
- The specific proof: uptime, price, coverage area.
- A direct call to action with the next step.
- Cut it when the headline already says what you sell.
whether you're
- The one reader you wrote for, named: "This guide is for developers who know Git and have never used rebase."
- Two paths with labels, if you serve two audiences: "New to Git: start at 2.1. Already use it: skip to 4."
- The actual limits: smallest and largest supported case, in numbers.
- Cut it when the poles are invented; pick the reader.
more than just
- The category, then the specific extra: "A to-do app with a shared calendar."
- What you do for the client, with a duration or count.
- The product facts: origin, roast, price.
- Cut it when the extra is a feeling; name a feature or drop the line.
imagine a world
- The current problem, stated with its cost.
- The proposed change and what it does now, not in an imagined world.
- The measured time, for "minutes not months" claims.
- Cut it when the next sentence is the product; start there.
picture this
- A real case, dated, with the details: who, when, what broke.
- The measured result, stated as fact.
- The feature in plain present tense.
- Cut it when the scenario is invented; use a real one or none.
here's the thing
- The point, as the first sentence.
- The fact placed with the others, at its normal weight.
- The cause and effect in one sentence with "because".
- Cut it every time; the clause after it stands alone.
the best part
- The fact in the place where readers look for it: price in the pricing line, requirements in the setup section.
- The list of integrations, named.
- The setup step count, for "no code" claims.
- Cut it when the reveal is one feature among several; list it with them.
i hope this helps
- The last step or the verification command, as the final line: "Run `npm test` to confirm."
- The one open question that changes the answer: "If you are on Node 16, use option B instead."
- In code comments, the reason for the code and nothing else.
- Cut it every time; end on the answer.
happy coding
- A next step link: "Next: add authentication (part 3)."
- In a script header, what the script does and how to run it.
- A summary of what is now running and where, for deploy guides.
- Cut it every time; the reader does not need a sign-off from a document.
feel free to
- The imperative, when you want the action: "Open an issue."
- A condition, when it depends: "If requests time out on slow networks, raise `timeout` to 30s."
- The process, for contributions: where, what format, who reviews.
- Cut it when it closes a chat answer; the user knows they can reply.
don't hesitate
- The channel and the response time: "Email support@ (reply within 1 working day)."
- A specific prompt for what to send: "Send the request ID from the error page."
- Nothing, when the reader already knows how to reply.
- Cut it when it closes an email; the reply button is enough.
great question
- The answer as the first sentence.
- If the question exposes a gap in docs, say so and link the fix: "The docs don't cover this; I added a section."
- In review replies, the answer or the change you made.
- Cut it every time.
as an ai
- The limit, stated as a fact about the task: "I have not run this code."
- What the reader can do to check: the command, the source, the date of the data.
- A recommendation with its reason, when asked for an opinion.
- Cut it when the sentence after it stands on its own.
i'd be happy to
- The work itself, from the first word: the query, the explanation, the function.
- A one-line clarifying question, if the request is ambiguous.
- A note of scope, when you will only do part: "This covers the login flow; signup is separate."
- Cut it every time.
crafted with
- The plain credit: "Made by a team of 4 in Berlin."
- The specific detail that shows care: test coverage, accessibility audit, support hours.
- The design rule, stated: "No setting has more than 2 options."
- Cut it from footers; the company name and year are enough.
designed with you in mind
- The audience, named, and one decision made for them.
- The user research behind a change: "After 30 interviews with nurses, we moved X."
- The specific change, described.
- Cut it when no audience or decision follows.
built for the future
- The support window: "Each major version gets 3 years of security fixes."
- The scaling limit tested: "tested to 10 TB and 50,000 writes per second".
- The exit path: export formats, open standards used.
- Cut it when no policy or test stands behind it.
the future of
- What the product does, as the headline: "Pay suppliers in 40 currencies from one account."
- The specific change in how people work, measured.
- The specific release and what it adds.
- Cut it when you cannot name the change.
with ease
- The step count or the time: "Deploy in one command."
- The specific sources, listed, for import claims.
- The verb alone, with the feature name.
- Cut it when there is no number for the ease.
made simple
- A verb headline that names what the user does: "Send an invoice in 30 seconds."
- The scope of the simplification: what was removed or automated.
- The audience and the outcome.
- Cut it when the noun is the whole tagline; write a sentence.
take your
- The result, measured: "Close tickets in half the time."
- What the certificate qualifies the reader to do, and its cost.
- The specific edit the tool makes.
- Cut it when there is no destination you can name.
in the world of
- The claim, scoped by a subject: "On e-commerce sites, each extra second of load time lowers conversion."
- The specific evidence for the generality.
- Nothing, if the field is the topic of the page.
- Cut it when the sentence after it is a platitude; cut the platitude too.
when it comes to
- The topic as the subject of the sentence: "Go compiles to one binary and starts in 10ms."
- The options, listed, for "many options" lines.
- The instruction, directly: "Write one test for the checkout total first."
- Cut it when the topic is already the subject of the paragraph.
the art of
- The skill as a task, with its scope: "How to split a 1,000-line PR into 4."
- The specific steps the guide teaches, named.
- The outcome the reader will have afterward.
- Cut it when the guide is a checklist; title it as one.
the heart of
- The policy or mechanism that shows the value: "We store no message content; it is encrypted on your device."
- The dependency fact: "Every job passes through the scheduler; if it stops, nothing runs."
- The location with a distance: "200m from Rossio station."
- Cut it when the value is not backed by a policy.
